input.question: why is the permeability of free space such a "clean " number?
input.ground_truth: Because we defined the amp as > the constant current that will produce an attractive force of 2 × 10^(−7) newtons per metre of length between two straight, parallel conductors of infinite length and negligible circular cross section placed one metre apart in a vacuum and so we end up with a clean number for the permeability of free space and a messy number for number of electrons needed for a charge of one coulomb. We could have defined a coulomb as, say, the charge of 10^18 electrons, an amp as one of those coulombs per second, and then the permeability of free space would be the messy number instead.

response.prediction:
Okay! Let’s imagine you have a big box of tiny, tiny marbles (these are like the "magnetic field lines" around a magnet). Now, sometimes you want to know how easily these marbles can go through something, like a sponge.

The "permeability of free space" is like a special rule that tells us how easily those marbles can move through *nothing*—just empty space, like the air around you.

Now, why is this rule such a "clean" number? Well, imagine if you had a magic sponge that was exactly the same everywhere, always the same size, and never changed. If you dropped marbles on it, they always went through the same way, every single time. That’s what "clean" means here—it’s the same, simple number everywhere in the universe, because empty space is always the same!

So, scientists found that this number is just a certain value (about 1.26 × 10⁻⁶), and it doesn’t change unless you put something else (like iron or water) in the way. That’s why it’s called a "clean" number—it’s simple and always the same in empty space.
